newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour to crack down on North Sea oil pollution.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour to crack down on North Sea oil pollution.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party said on Monday waste from oil and gas rigs was creating "biological deserts" in the North Sea and vowed to step up monitoring of offshore installations if it comes to power.
But the government's Trade and Industry department accused it of exaggerating the scale of the problem and failing to acknowledge measures already being undertaken to tackle it.
Michael Meacher, Labour's environmental protection spokesman, accused the government of failing to apply European Union regulations designed to minimise the impact of oil companies' operations.
"The government have shown no real concern for the problem whatever," Meacher said in a statement.

"There are too few inspections, proper records are not kept, companies are never prosecuted, information is kept secret and licences are let without proper consideration of the environmental consequences."

Meacher said he had evidence that the operation of oil rigs in the British sector of the North Sea had led to the dumping of 1.5 million tonnes of waste on the sea bottom consisting largely of barium sulphate, but including 166,000 tonnes of oil.

"An area of 500 metres (yards) radius around each waste site is now a biological desert, and serious damage has been observed to sea life up to a radius of several kilometres (miles)," a note issued by his office said.

Meacher contrasted the attitude of the Norwegian authorities, who insisted on environmental assessments before rigs were allowed to operate, with Britain, which he said was ignoring EU regulations requiring such assessments.
He said Labour would implement the EU standards in the next round of North Sea licensing expected in the British sector later this year if it wins a general election due within the next four months.

It would also insist that government inspectors who monitor oil firms' compliance with environmental standards should stop announcing their visits to rigs in advance, and should become more willing to prosecute offenders.
In addition, Labour would make oil firms publish their environmental policies.
But a spokesman for the government's Trade and Industry department said in fact the amount of oil on the seabed was estimated at 68,000 tonnes, and this was being naturally degraded by bacteria.

He said it was impractical for security reasons for inspectors to make unannounced visits to oil rigs. But the government also monitored the industry through sensitive equipment on aircraft to detect oil floating on the sea.
Just 84 tonnes of oil had been detected in this way in 1995.

The spokesman said the government already required environmental assessments where drilling would have a significant impact, and planned to bring in legislation before the next drilling round to make this statutory.

However, environmental campaigners welcomed Meacher's statement. "His proposals would certainly help. At the moment the oil industry is almost completely self-regulatory," said Simon Reddy of the Greenpeace pressure group.
